messages.author: b30c14c8b83478cb
messages.subject: Replication for Bugs to Stan
parts:
Hello everyone,

I'm conducting a replication of an analysis that was originally conducted in Bugs. I'm looking to reproduce the Bugs model in Stan exactly, but I'm having some difficulty with its translation. In particular, I'm unclear how to reproduce the following from Bugs:

for(j in 1:10) {
  tau_j[j] ~ dgamma(0.1, 0.1)
}

for(i in 1:N) {
  tau_i[i] ~ dgamma(a, b)
}

a ~ dgamma(0.1, 0.1)
b ~ dgamma(0.1, 0.1)

To reproduce this, I have coded it as follows in Stan:

transformed parameters {
  real tau_j[n_j];
  real tau_i[n_i];

  for(m in 1:n_j) tau_j[m] = sqrt(tau_j_raw[m]);
  for(m in 1:n_i) tau_i[m] = sqrt(tau_i_raw[m]);

}


model {

tau_j_raw ~ inv_gamma(0.1, 0.1);


a ~ gamma(0.1, 0.1);
b ~ gamma(0.1, 0.1);
tau_i_raw ~ inv_gamma(a, b);

...

}

I feel like I might have something wrong with the multi-level parameters for tau_i_raw, but I'm not sure given my relative unfamiliarity with Bugs. Any help correcting (or verifying) this would be extremely useful.

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Replication for Bugs to Stan
parts:
It makes sense to try to replicate things.  But moving forward I recommend forgetting about these gamma distributions and just modeling the tau parameters directly.  Those inverse-gammas were only there in the Bugs model for convenience; they never made any statistical sense.  Now that they're not convenient either, you can get rid of them.
A

messages.author: b30c14c8b83478cb
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Replication for Bugs to Stan
parts:
Andrew:

Thank you for your response. Would you have any recommendation for modeling the variances here hierarchically? In the model below, the tau_i are individual-specific variances which are estimated from very few per-individual observations, hence the need for some structure.


Daniel:

Sure thing...

Bugs:

model {
for(i in 1:N) {
  for(j in 1:q) {
    z[i,j] ~ dnorm(mu[i,j], tau[i,j])
    mu[i,j] <- a[i] + b[i] * zhat[j]
    tau[i,j] <- tauj[j] * taui[i]
  }
}

for(i in 1:N) {
  a[i] ~ dunif(-100, 100)
  b[i] ~ dunif(-100, 100)
}

for(j in 1:q) {
  tauj[j] ~ dgamma(.1,.1)
}

for(i in 1:N) {
  taui[i] ~ dgamma(ga,gb)
}

ga ~ dgamma(.1,.1)
gb ~ dgamma(.1,.1)

zhat[1] ~ dnorm(0,1)T(0.9,1.1)
zhat[2] ~ dnorm(0,1)T(-1.1,-0.9)
for (j in 3:q) {
  zhat[j] ~ dnorm(0,1)
}

sigmai.sq <- 1/taui
sigmaj.sq <- 1/tauj

}

Stan:

data {

  int n_j;
  int n_i;
  int n_obs;

  int i[n_obs];
  int j[n_obs];
  real z[n_obs];

}

parameters {

  vector[n_i] a;
  vector[n_i] b;

  vector<lower = 0.9, upper = 1.1>[1] zeta_raw1;
  vector<lower = -1.1, upper = -0.9>[1] zeta_raw2;
  vector[n_j-2] zeta_raw;

  real<lower = 0> tau_j_raw[n_j];
  real<lower = 0> tau_i_raw[n_i];
  real<lower = 0> ga;
  real<lower = 0> gb;

}


transformed parameters {

  vector[n_j] zeta;

real tau_j[n_j];
  real tau_i[n_i];

zeta[1] = zeta_raw1[1];
  zeta[2] = zeta_raw2[1];
  for(m in 3:n_j) zeta[m] = zeta_raw[m-2];

for(m in 1:n_j) tau_j[m] = sqrt(tau_j_raw[m]);
  for(m in 1:n_i) tau_i[m] = sqrt(tau_i_raw[m]);

}


model {

// Priors
  a ~ uniform(-100, 100);
  b ~ uniform(-100, 100);

  zeta_raw1 ~ normal(0, 1);
  zeta_raw2 ~ normal(0, 1);
  zeta_raw ~ normal(0, 1);

  tau_j_raw ~ inv_gamma(0.1, 0.1);

  ga ~ gamma(0.1, 0.1);
  gb ~ gamma(0.1, 0.1);
  tau_i_raw ~ inv_gamma(ga, gb);

  // Likelihood
  for(m in 1:n_obs) {
      z[m] ~ normal(a[i[m]] + b[i[m]] * zeta[j[m]], tau_j[j[m]] * tau_i[i[m]]);
  }

}

parts:
Some quick comments:
- Get rid of those uniform distributions.
- Make sure the parameters are on roughly unit scale
- Use hierarchical model rather than flat priors for a and b.
- You can use half-normal priors for the scale parameters.  Model scales, not variances or inverse-variances.
- Those [.9, 1.1] constraints look like bad ideas also.  If you want to put in prior info, use soft constraints.

messages.author: b30c14c8b83478cb
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Replication for Bugs to Stan
parts:
Thanks for this Andrew.

In a previous edit to the model, I had done all of what you suggest here. The [0.9, 1.1] and [-1.1, -0.9] constraints appeared to be problematic because the posterior distribution of the associated parameters were bumping up heavily against -0.9 and 0.9 respectively. I also put hierarchical priors on a and b instead of uniforms.

The only problem computationally was using normals on the scale parameters. The tau_i are multiplied by the tau_j in the likelihood to account for heteroskedastic error, but with normal priors I couldn't get model convergence. I'll be looking into that more shortly. At the moment, because I'm using the replication as my baseline model, I'm aiming to replicate it exactly in Stan as it was set up in Bugs.

is, you just have to define things before they're used.
Then you can get it to work and start making it more
efficient.

If you have uniform distributions on a parameter, it
needs to be declared with the same bounds (using upper= and
lower=).

What we do recommend for priors is in the manual and on
a wiki page on stan-dev on GitHub.

Out of curiousity, why does the original model multiply
precisions (or in Stan terms, you wind up multiplying
scales)?

> for(i in 1:N) {
> for(j in 1:q) {

> z[i,j] ~ dnorm(mu[i,j], tau[i,j])
> mu[i,j] <- a[i] + b[i] * zhat[j]
> tau[i,j] <- tauj[j] * taui[i]
- Bob

parts:
Hi Bob,

Thanks for this.

I tried to code the original Bugs program in Stan as directly as possible (as above). Everything in the transformed variables block is there to accommodate constraints in Stan that work differently from those in Bugs. For example, as I understand it, one can't (yet) put lower and upper constraints on only one element of a vector (hence the zeta_raw1, zeta_raw2, zeta_raw). And because Bugs uses precision, the parameters that are distributed dgamma(·) in Bugs need to be changed to 1 / sqrt(·).

The scales get multiplied because the model is for a object placement scale. Individuals may differ in their ability to place an item, and some items are more difficult to place than others. So the idea is to capture heterogeneous error (varying at both the individual and item level).

The Stan code above doesn't behave well though. The rhats are all very large and the n_eff extremely low. I suspect it's something in how I've coded from Bugs to Stan, but I can't make it out.

parts:
I think this is the model you want:

data {
int<lower=0> N;
int<lower=0> Q;
matrix[N, Q] z;
}
parameters {
vector<lower=-100, upper=100>[N] a;
vector<lower=-100, upper=100>[N] b;
real<lower=0.9, upper=1.1> zhat1_raw;
real<lower=-1.1, upper=-0.9> zhat2_raw;
real[Q-2] zhat3_Q_raw;
vector<lower=0>[N] taui;
vector<lower=0>[Q] tauj;
}
transformed parameters {
real sigmai = 1 / sqrt(taui);
real sigmaj = 1 / sqrt(tauj);
vector[Q] z_hat;
z_hat[1] = zhat1_raw;
z_hat[2] = zhat2_raw;
z_hat[3:Q] = zhat3_Q_raw;
}
model {

ga ~ gamma(0.1, 0.1);
gb ~ gamma(0.1, 0.1);

taui ~ gamma(ga, gb);
tauj ~ gamma(0.1, 0.1);
z_hat ~ normal(0, 1);
for (i in 1:N)
for (j in 1:Q)
z[i, j] ~ normal(a[i] + b[i] * zhat[j], tauj[j] * taui[i]);
}

translation of the BUGS code you sent.
